title: How the Torah is read
hookLine: a handwritten scroll, read aloud on Shabbat, Mondays and Thursdays

lines: WHEN IT COMES OUT, PEOPLE STAND.
cards: Most books are printed by a machine, thousands of copies at once. This one never is. Every letter is written by hand, with a quill, in ink, on parchment, by a trained scribe, one letter at a time.
It's rolled on two wooden poles, dressed in a cloth cover, and kept in a cabinet at the front of the synagogue. When it comes out, people stand.
Some reach out to touch it with the fringe of a prayer shawl, then kiss the fringe. And then someone reads it out loud, in a chant handed down from teacher to student.

teach.b: Sefer Torah means a book of Torah: the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written by a sofer, a scribe, on sheets of parchment sewn together. The rules are exacting.
Every letter must be formed correctly, and a single missing or broken letter can make the scroll unfit until it's fixed.

teach.h: NO VOWELS, A POINTER CALLED A YAD.
teach.b: There are no vowels in it and no punctuation, so the reader learns ahead of time how the words sound.

The reader doesn't touch the parchment with a finger, but follows the line with a yad, a small pointer, often shaped like a hand. And it's chanted aloud in a set melody, with marks passed down for each word. When?
On Shabbat morning, a full weekly portion. On Monday and Thursday mornings, and Shabbat afternoon, a shorter piece. Why Monday and Thursday?

The Talmud connects it to the Israelites in the wilderness, who went three days without water and grew weak. The sages compared Torah to water, and arranged the readings so that three days never pass without it.
Public reading appears in the Bible itself.

In the book of Nehemiah, Ezra the scribe stands on a wooden platform and reads the Torah aloud to the whole people, men, women and all who could understand, and teachers explain it so everyone follows.
In the synagogue, Torah isn't read silently in a corner. It's heard, together, out loud, with the whole room listening.

how: In synagogues the Torah scroll is taken from the ark and chanted aloud on Shabbat morning and afternoon and on Monday and Thursday mornings, as well as on festivals; the reader follows the text with a pointer called a yad.

games.q: you're the reader. the scroll is open, the letters are small, and you need to keep your place. what do you use?
o: a printed copy on top of the scroll.
games.why: a yad. the reader doesn't touch the parchment with a finger; the pointer, often shaped like a hand, keeps the place.

practice: Close your eyes, and for this minute read nothing: just listen to the sounds around you, near and far.
Then remember a voice that once read to you, a parent at bedtime, a teacher, anyone, and hear the words the way you heard them then.
